title: Portage and Path Dependence
research_question: Does the historical distribution of economic activity persist at locations whose original natural advantages have become obsolete, and if so, why do such population centers continue to thrive long after the features that first attracted settlement have lost their value? Specifically, can initial, now-obsolete locational advantages have lasting effects on the spatial distribution of population and economic activity, and what role do sunk historical investments versus increasing returns to scale play in generating this persistence?
data_description: The study combines several spatial datasets at the U.S. county, census tract, and sub-tract levels. Decennial county population data (1790-2000) come from Haines's census compilations, normalized to consistent boundaries using NHGIS shapefiles. Census 2000 tract populations measure contemporary density at high spatial frequency, supplemented with 2003 nighttime light intensity from satellite photos as a continuous activity measure. Historical portage sites are identified using the U.S. Geological Survey's fall-line layer intersected with major rivers, plus historical documents on Midwest fur-trader portages and 19th-century Army Corps river surveys. Additional variables include climate (Climate Atlas), elevation, aquifers, 1885 water-power potential, 18th-century seaports, 1890 river navigability, 1850 railroads (Atack et al.), and historical factor measures (literacy, sectoral employment, college teachers) from IPUMS census microdata 1850-1930. Wage regressions use 2000 IPUMS workers aged 25-65 in fall-line metropolitan areas.
institutional_context: During North American settlement, long-distance goods movement was largely waterborne, and portage sites—where boats had to be unloaded and carried overland around rapids, falls, or between watersheds—became natural focal points for commerce, transshipment, and supporting services. In the southeastern and Mid-Atlantic United States, the fall line, a geomorphological boundary between the Piedmont and coastal plain, marked the last rapids before rivers reached the Atlantic or Gulf, generating a string of portage towns (e.g., Richmond, Augusta, Philadelphia, Trenton). Similar portages existed between the Great Lakes and Mississippi system (Chicago, South Bend) and along Mississippi tributaries (Louisville at the Falls of the Ohio). Beginning in the early-to-mid 1800s, canals, locks, and especially railroads eliminated the need for transshipment around these obstacles, while cheaper power sources later displaced water power. By 1890, most fall-line rivers were no longer used for significant commercial shipping, rendering the original portage advantage obsolete.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treatment = counties with historical portage sites, control = counties without portage sites; shock/instrument/cutoff = historical necessity of portage

key_variables.treatment: presence of a historical portage site in a county
key_variables.control: absence of a historical portage site in a county
key_variables.outcome: current economic activity, urbanization, population density
key_variables.time_period: historical data from 18th/19th centuries to present

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Counties with historical portage sites exhibit higher levels of economic activity and urbanization today.
